require_first_item_under_heading.heading: boildown
require_first_item_under_heading.matching: ^\s*the work of this session is now on\s*:
require_first_item_under_heading.why: The Boildown opens with where the work is and which of the five stages it finished -- "The work of this session is now on: <branch> (you have finished step N of 5, <Stage>)" -- in every reply, a plan-only one included (no branch yet, step 1 of 5, Consider).

why: Morgan, 2026-09-29 (strength: decided): the first bullet after the Boildown heading names the branch this session's work is on and the stage it has finished, with no exception. Blocking, like the heading beside it, because it is structural: the line is either first under the heading or it is not, and a line meant for every reply is the kind a session drops when the rest of the reply feels finished.

require_in_fence_paired_with.why: a paste block that tells another session to land, merge, push or open a pull request onto pre-staging, staging or main, or says the same in other words (a stage word as the order, make it live, ship it, merge the PR, --promote, gh pr merge, git push origin main) carries landing authority, and only the person's own Booked (or Approved, Go update) for this handoff gives it -- quoted in the block, so the receiving session can check it. Without that word, the prompt ends at Act: build on the feature branch, push it there, and stop

why: 2026-10-01: two prompts a session wrote ended 'Land it on staging per this repo's conventions'. Morgan had not said Booked, and routine work lands on pre-staging, never staging. fence-block-for-paste passed both, because it checks that a block says where it goes, not what it authorizes. Morgan: 'No, we always want to do it in the local container ("Act") and then I'll authorize it to go to pre-staging via "Promote" etc.' 2026-10-08: a block that ends at the feature branch may NARRATE a past landing (a session or tool did it, past tense, no 'you') without being read as an order (BestPractice tools/precedent_reply_check.py, narration_exempt_if_block_matches). Later on 2026-10-08: the trigger skipped any LINE holding do not/never/no/without, so 'Merge it into main, no questions asked' passed with nobody's Booked. A negator now exempts a clause only when it governs the landing verb in that clause (BestPractice tools/precedent_reply_check.py, negation_exempt_if_clause_negates), and also_if_matches lists the other ways a block says land. Morgan: 'shouldn't it understand the intent behind commands not just the literal words?' (practice: read-for-intent, BestPractice). An engine older than that ignores both keys: it judges every negated line, the stricter reading, and enforces if_matches alone.

Morgan, 2026-10-09: "I want to make sure there's a full check *somewhere* on the push to main, afterwards" -- with four exceptions: GitHub's test runs on it, Debut passed on exactly this, only prose changed, or he asked for a fast one. A merged fast move that owes the full local suite on main holds the turn until it has started, and while it has failed.
